covers.quote: Remember to avoid blocks of italics wherever possible. Blocks of italics are difficult to read, so consider other formatting and design options.

rules.specification: more than a paragraph or a few lines of continuous text in italics
rules.violation_condition: a large block or chunk of text formatted in italics
rules.why: G-4: The instruction 'Avoid chunks of italic text' acts as the most complete statement of this rule, absorbing the fragmented list item and later restatements.

rules.quote: material that would normally be in italics but is set apart (such as a list of titles under a heading)
rules.violation_condition: italics applied to a list of titles or other normally-italicised material when it is set apart as a block or list
rules.why: G-1: A child list item defining a specific context where formatting rules change and italics must not be used.

rules.quote: aggregation pages (such as a page listing legislation/type(principal)/collection(act))).
rules.specification: pages that solely list links to other items
rules.violation_condition: italics used on an aggregation page
rules.why: G-1: A specific exclusion for web aggregation pages, stated as a list item.

covers.quote: Unpublished works are in roman type.
Don’t use italics for the titles of sacred texts, such as the Bible or the Koran.
A title or name in italic type shows that it is formal and complete. Shortened versions of the title and common titles are in roman type. Follow the detailed guidance for referencing and attribution.

examples.note: Demonstrates the contrast between a publication (needs italics) and an award (no italics).

parts.quote: The Australian of the Year honour is a government award. It is different from The Australian’s annual award of the same name. [Publication titles use italics, but not awards.]

examples.note: Example of italicised play title (italics missing in markdown text but implied).

parts.quote: David Williamson’s play Emerald city was first performed in 1987.

examples.note: Example of musical composition title.

parts.quote: Elena Kats-Chernin’s Piano concerto no. 3is a recent work by the award-winning composer.

examples.note: Example of artwork title.

parts.quote: In 2018, Yvette Coppersmith won the Archibald Prize with Self-portrait, after George Lambert.

rules.quote: Use italics for the titles of these published works:
rules.violation_condition: the title of a published work (such as a book, play, periodical, film, or artwork) written in roman type
when: The work is published; unpublished works are in roman type
The work is not a sacred text such as the Bible or the Koran
Shortened versions of the title and common titles are in roman type
rules.why: G-1: The list of published work types and their exceptions defines the extent of this rule.

examples.note: Demonstrates reverse italics.

parts.quote: Gone onThe Ghanand other great railway journeys of Australia [The Ghan is the official name of a train; it would normally be italicised.]

rules.quote: In some titles, there are words that would normally be italicised. To make sure they stand out from the rest of the italicised title, write the words in roman type.
rules.violation_condition: a word within an italicised title that normally takes italics (like a nested title) formatted in italics instead of roman type
rules.why: G-4: Replaces the candidate heading 'Reverse italics in titles of published works' with the sentence that describes the action.

examples.note: Shows the appropriate formatting for cases, bills, and acts in context.

parts.quote: The Franklin Dam Case is the informal title of Commonwealth v Tasmania (1983) 158 CLR 1. The case led to the World Heritage Properties Conservation Bill which became an Act in 1983. In 1999, the Act was replaced by parts of the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999.
[The case name and the Act are italicised; the name for the bill, before enacted, is in roman type.]

rules.quote: Use italics for primary legislation and legal cases but not for delegated legislation or bills.
rules.violation_condition: the title of primary legislation or a legal case written in roman type, or the title of delegated legislation or a bill written in italics
rules.why: G-2: Consolidates formatting for different types of legal documents into a single rule.

covers.quote: Italics contrast words and phrases that are not in English from surrounding text. Foreign words and phrases should generally be avoided in government writing, unless there is no English equivalent.
Standard Australian English can absorb words or phrases from other languages. Write these ‘borrowed’ words without italics or accent marks.
Do not italicise names or words from First Nations languages. They are Australian languages, not foreign languages.

examples.note: Foreign phrase italicised.

parts.quote: The more things change, plus c’est la même.

examples.note: Borrowed word 'barista' correctly in roman type.

parts.quote: John was the head barista at the department’s coffee shop.

rules.quote: Set off most foreign words and phrases
rules.violation_condition: a foreign word or phrase written without italics
when: The word or phrase has no English equivalent
The word is not a 'borrowed' word absorbed into Standard Australian English
The word or name is not from a First Nations language
rules.why: G-2: Brings together the main rule for foreign phrases and the exceptions for borrowed words and First Nations languages.

parts.quote: The abbreviation ‘cf.’ is from the Latin word confer and means ‘compare’.

rules.quote: Write the full Latin word in italics but not the shortened form.
rules.violation_condition: a Latin shortened form (such as 'etc.' or 'i.e.') written in italics, or a full Latin word written in roman type
rules.why: G-4: The sentence provides the precise wording instead of the candidate heading.

rules.quote: Instead, to draw attention to words with special meaning, use single quotation marks.
rules.specification: looks for first-use definitions in italics instead of single quotes
rules.violation_condition: italics used to define or introduce a technical term or draw attention to words with special meaning
rules.why: G-4: Rule instructing against the common convention of using italics for newly introduced terms.

parts.quote: Pythagoras’s theorem for a right-angled triangle proved that a2 + b2 = c2.

rules.quote: Specialist uses of italics include well-known mathematical theorems and formulas.
rules.violation_condition: a well-known mathematical theorem or formula written in roman type
rules.why: Specific requirement for formatting mathematical content.

parts.quote: Until 1997, Queen Elizabeth II would use the Britannia to sail to official visits overseas. [The definite article ‘the’ is in roman type, while the ship’s official name is in italics.]
Qantas uses Australian names like Great Southern Land for the Dreamliner fleet.

rules.quote: The name is in italics excluding any definite article. The brand or type of vehicle is in roman type.
rules.violation_condition: the proper name of a ship, train, aircraft or other vehicle written in roman type, or the definite article or brand/type written in italics
rules.why: Consolidates rules for formatting official names of vehicles.

covers.quote: Write the scientific names of infectious organisms, including some bacteria and fungi, in italics.

parts.quote: Acacia phlebocarpa is the scientific name for the tabletop wattle.
Certain strains of the bacteria Staphylococcus aureus cause golden staph.

rules.quote: Use italics for the genus and species, including any subspecies, but not for the common name.
rules.violation_condition: a scientific name of a plant, animal or infectious organism written in roman type, or a common name written in italics
rules.why: G-2: Merges general scientific names formatting with the specific inclusion of infectious organisms.

covers.quote: Sometimes you want to stress a word for meaning or to convey emotion, including a change in tone. Italics, used sparingly, can work for this purpose.

examples.note: Demonstrates emphasis using italics as a last resort in dialogue.

parts.quote: ‘I didn’t mean her,’ they said, ‘I meant him.’

examples.note: Demonstrates emphasis.

parts.quote: The deadline is Monday, not Friday.

rules.quote: Don’t use italics when another style or formatting option is available. Single quotation marks can work for emphasis unless they’re serving a different stylistic use.
rules.specification: Requires context to identify emphasis versus titles or foreign words.
rules.violation_condition: italics used for emphasis when another style such as single quotation marks would suffice
rules.why: G-3: The permission to sparingly use italics for emphasis is absorbed into the primary guideline that advises avoiding them in favour of other options.

parts.quote: ‘Subsequently, in 1903, Parliament passed a unanimous resolution that it should be flown.’ [emphasis added]

rules.quote: If you do this, write ‘emphasis added’ in square brackets following the italicised text.
rules.violation_condition: a quotation with italics added for emphasis that lacks '[emphasis added]' following the text
rules.why: Specific formatting requirement when modifying a quotation with emphasis.

rules.quote: If the italics is part of the original text, write ‘emphasis from original’ in the square brackets following the quotation.
rules.violation_condition: a quotation with original italics that lacks '[emphasis from original]' following the text
rules.why: Specific formatting requirement for quoting text containing italics.
